whatsHappening.background: The Kurds are one of the world’s largest stateless peoples, living mainly across Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria. After World War I, the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres raised the possibility of Kurdish autonomy, but the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne left Kurds divided across new state borders. Since then, Kurdish communities have faced shifting repression, armed conflict, displacement, and denied political rights in different countries.

civilianImpact.experiences: For Kurdish civilians, the crisis has meant displacement, village destruction, chemical attacks, language and identity restrictions, detention, and repeated insecurity. The impact differs by country, but the pattern is similar: Kurdish communities are often caught between state security campaigns, armed groups, foreign alliances, and broader wars.

image.alt: Map showing Kurdish-inhabited areas across the region

whatsHappening.background: Kurdish civilians are affected by conflict in several overlapping ways: displacement from military campaigns, loss of homes, restrictions on language and political organizing, and violence from both state forces and armed groups. In Iraq, Anfal and Halabja remain defining traumas. In Syria, ISIS and later Turkish-backed offensives displaced many Kurdish families.

civilianImpact.experiences: Civilian harm is not only physical violence. It also includes losing homes, being forced into camps, being separated by borders, and facing pressure over Kurdish language, identity, and political participation. Because Kurdish communities are divided across several states, the crisis is often fragmented and easier for the world to overlook.

whatsHappening.background: Helping Kurdish civilians means supporting people across several countries rather than one single state. Aid can help displaced families in Iraq and Syria, while awareness can keep attention on rights abuses, press freedom, cultural restrictions, and the long-term effects of conflict.

timeline.description: Understand Kurdish history and why state borders matter.
Use credible reporting and avoid flattening all Kurds into one group.
Donate to trusted relief groups working in Iraq, Syria, and nearby areas.

civilianImpact.experiences: Support should center civilians: displaced families, survivors of past atrocities, communities affected by cross-border attacks, and people facing repression for Kurdish identity or politics. Because the crisis is spread across borders, reliable information and trusted humanitarian aid both matter.

howToHelp.summary: Use the support options on the right to donate through broad humanitarian groups, then keep learning from reliable reporting about Kurdish civilians across Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria.

learnMore.text: Follow trusted human rights reporting, Kurdish civil society voices, and humanitarian updates from the region.
